newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK credit/house data shows confidence back.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK credit/house data shows confidence back.

text.p: British house prices jumped 1.7 percent in August and consumer credit topped a billion pounds ($1.56 billion) in July, figures out on Friday showed, providing the government with welcome evidence that the "feel-good" factor is returning.
The government pounced on the figures as evidence that consumers are feeling more secure about the future.
William Waldegrave, chief secretary to the Treasury, said they showed consumers "are increasingly confident on their prospects and the outlook for the economy as a whole."
The Nationwide Building Society's house price index showed property prices are now 5.4 percent higher than last August and at their highest level since August 1991.
"Prices have risen every month so far this year," said Nationwide's corporate development director Philip Williamson.
"With steady increases expected to continue into the autumn, we will see house prices at the end of this year at least five percent higher than at the end of 1995."
House prices are an important barometer of consumer confidence in Britain, where two-thirds of households own their homes.
July's credit figures showed consumers are clearly feeling the benefit of lower interest rates and higher house prices.
The Bank of England said consumers borrowed 1.027 billion pounds in the month, well above expectations on financial markets, compared with 659 million pounds in June.
"The figures suggest confidence is improving rapidly and... consumers have re-embarked on another borrowing binge," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS.
But the surge in borrowing means there is less room for the government to cut the cost of borrowing in the autumn.
"The data confirm the picture of a consumer-led recovery in the economy," said Jeremy Hawkins, economist at Bank of America. "As such, they argue against further cuts in interest rates."

The ruling Conservatives, who are lagging the opposition Labour Party by over 20 points in opinion polls, are eager to restore a strong sense of national well-being before the general election, which must be held by May 1997.
British voters are particularly sensitive to the level of interest rates because most home loans are variable-rate.

There is speculation that Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke will cut the cost of borrowing again to give the economy, and the government's electoral chances, one last push.

Interest rates have been cut four times since December and stand at 5.75 percent. Clarke and Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George, who has warned against further rate cuts, hold their monthly monetary meeting next Wednesday.
Economists said Clarke could face a full-blown argument with the central bank and an adverse reaction on financial markets if he pushed through another rate cut.
There are already fears that the consumer-led recovery could become a runaway spending boom if monetary policy is too lax.
However, the Nationwide was adamant that although the housing market is recovering, there is no chance of an early repetition of the 1980s property boom.
"We still feel that any talk of a damaging boom in prices is seriously misplaced. It should be remembered that values in some regions are still 30 percent below their 1980s peak," said Williamson.
